# Force Based Gamemastering #

### A guide to help you run reactive non-linear campaigns ###

## Table of Contents ##

1. [Introduction: Why This Guide Exists](#introduction-why-this-guide-exists)
2. [Part I: What I’m Trying to Create](#part-i-what-im-trying-to-create)
3. [Part II: Setting Up the Game](#part-ii-setting-up-the-game)

## Introduction: Why This Guide Exists ##

### Why I'm Writing This ###

Much of the campaign-creation advice I've encountered seems to lead to campaigns that feel dead to me: either the game is pushed along a predetermined track, or the GM is left stranded when the characters do something nobody could have predicted. I don't want to predict what the characters will do. I want enough understanding of the situation to make decisions in real time that feel like they belong in the same world and story.

This guide is my attempt to capture how I do that. I build a small number of forces with goals, limits, and recognizable fingerprints, then consider how they relate to one another and to the characters. I prepare heavily at the beginning—often spending most of that preparation developing the forces—and much less after play begins. That initial work gives me a model of the situation, not a sequence of events I expect the players to follow.

At the table, I use that model to improvise. The forces pursue their goals; the characters interfere, cooperate, or do something I never anticipated; and the situation changes in response. I try to follow what the players find entertaining without deciding outcomes in advance. The aim is improvisation that stays coherent: the world can surprise us without feeling arbitrary, and the story can change without losing its continuity or tone.

### What This Guide Will—and Won't—Teach ###

This is a style of play built around a substantial initial investment and low-maintenance preparation afterward. It is meant to help a GM follow the joy of the table and improvise freely, while giving them enough understanding to keep the campaign feeling cohesive.

It is not a formula for producing a successful campaign. The ideas here are rules of thumb, not laws. They can—and should—be changed to fit the circumstances, and understanding why a rule of thumb exists matters more than following it mechanically. This approach cannot guarantee that a game will be fun, remove the GM's responsibility for story design, or prevent every improvised choice from disrupting continuity or even breaking the story. It offers tools that can help prevent those problems and help a GM respond when the unexpected happens.

### Who This Approach Might Suit ###

I'm writing this first to capture my own thoughts so I can review and refine them. Eventually, I hope to publish the guide freely on the web. I especially hope it will help new Gamemasters, and that some of its techniques will inspire the people writing books about running games.

This approach may suit a GM who enjoys responding to players more than steering them toward a planned sequence, but still wants the world to feel consistent. It may also suit someone willing to spend time developing a campaign before play in exchange for having less to prepare between sessions. It won't be the right fit for every GM or every table; the point is to understand the approach well enough to decide what is useful for yours.

### How to Use This Guide ###

Skim the guide first to get a sense of the whole approach, then read more deeply wherever a chapter is useful to you. You don't need to adopt every rule of thumb. As you read, consider why I use each one, what it is meant to accomplish, and what might need to change for your group.

The examples show what these ideas have looked like in my games, not what every campaign should look like. I always begin with combat created by the collision of forces' actions. The characters may be caught in the fallout rather than fighting those forces directly. That is one way I put the campaign in motion; the larger principle is to create a situation with energy and connections, then let play determine what happens next.

## Part I: What I’m Trying to Create ##

* [What a Good Game Looks Like to Me](#what-a-good-game-looks-like-to-me)

### What a Good Game Looks Like to Me ###

#### What I Want Players to Experience ####

I want the game to feel like a good carnival ride: adrenaline, exhaustion, excitement, and real emotion. I want everyone at the table to have a good time.

My biggest sign that a game has worked is what the players do when it ends. Either they don't want to leave, or they leave rehashing what happened. That energy—the desire to stay in the experience or to keep talking about it afterward—is what I look for.

#### What Makes a Session Feel Successful ####

A session is successful when the players are engaged enough that they want more, or when the events keep mattering to them after the session is over. It doesn't have to follow the plan or advance a predetermined plot. The characters can surprise me, the situation can change, and the session can still feel cohesive.

I use preparation to help me respond to what happens, not to decide in advance what must happen. Forces pursue their goals and react to the characters; the characters' choices affect the situation. That gives play momentum while leaving the outcome open.

#### What I Prioritize When I Can't Have Everything ####

The table's fun is the only thing I will not sacrifice. Everything else can give way: the plot, the characters, the NPCs, the current TTRPG system, and more.

If the dice are getting in the way, I throw them out and play make-believe instead. Whatever works for the table is more important than continuing to use a rule or tool that is making the game less fun.

#### What I'm Comfortable Leaving Out ####

I'm comfortable leaving out or changing anything that gets in the way of the table's fun. I don't need to preserve a planned plot, protect an NPC from the consequences of play, or keep using a system just because we started with it.

This doesn't mean I don't care about continuity, characters, or the story. I use preparation and the campaign's forces to help keep events coherent while improvising. But those are ways to support the experience, not obligations that outrank it.

### The GM's Job—and Its Limits ###

#### What I Take Responsibility For ####

I technically have authority over the forces and the world's reactions, but I don't think of myself as standing above the table. I think of myself as its steward. My job is to help create and maintain a situation the table can enjoy, and to respond to what happens without forcing the game down a predetermined path.

That includes making calls in the moment. I use the forces, their goals and limits, and what has already happened to make the world's responses feel like they belong. I also take responsibility for making the game safe enough for everyone at the table to participate.

#### What I Leave to the Players ####

I don't try to predict what the characters will do or require them to follow a planned sequence. The players decide what their characters attempt, and those choices can change the campaign. If a character's action is vetoed for safety, I work with that player to find a different action rather than leaving them without a way forward.

#### What We Decide Together ####

Safety is the ultimate authority at my table. As a group, we decide what can initially go into the game and when it can happen. During play, every player has veto power over content, no questions asked. This is my one hard rule.

When someone uses a veto, the offending context is removed. I make a note, and after the session the only question I ask is whether I recorded it correctly so it can be added to our banned-topics list. The veto does not require explanation or discussion in the moment.

The table's fun is shared, too. I am a member of the table, and my enjoyment matters as much as any one player's. I find enjoyment in doing something well, so I'm willing to throw out the plot, characters, NPCs, or even the system if that is what the table needs. I recommend that prospective GMs figure out what makes GMing enjoyable for them and find a group that wants that kind of game. I usually ask my players to help us find our fun together. If we can't, I end the game; if one person at the table isn't having fun, it tends to tank the whole table.

#### How Authority Works at My Table ####

My authority over the forces and the world's reactions is practical, not absolute. I use it in service of the table, and I don't use it to overrule a safety veto or protect my planned story. If there is a conflict about a rule or a ruling, I bring it to a table vote and move on.

For ordinary rules questions, I use this loose framework:

1. **I don't know the rule:** The player can do it for now. I let them know I'll look it up for future sessions.
2. **The character probably can't do it, but the attempt is plausible:** They can do it, perhaps with a slight increase in difficulty.
3. **The action is too outlandish for the character:** I use “No, but.” I say no to that specific action, then discuss other ways the character could accomplish their goal.

If the dice are getting in the way of the table's fun, I set them aside and play make-believe instead. Rules and systems are tools; they don't outrank the people playing.

### The Principles Behind My Decisions ###

#### My Core Principles ####

##### Safety is the hard boundary #####

The table decides what content is acceptable, and every player can veto content at any time without explanation. Nothing about a plot, encounter, or character takes priority over that.

##### The table's fun comes first #####

The table's fun is the one thing I will not sacrifice. Plot, characters, NPCs, and even the game system are all things I can change or discard if they get in the way. I am part of the table, too, so I look for a kind of play we can enjoy together.

##### Prepare situations, not outcomes #####

I put substantial effort into the initial campaign concepts, especially the forces: what they want, what they will and will not do, and how their actions can be recognized. I use this preparation to understand the situation, not to predict what the characters will do or dictate what must happen.

##### Let play change the situation #####

The characters' actions matter. Forces pursue their goals, react to interference, and may change as the campaign develops. I follow what the table finds engaging rather than insisting that players pursue every prepared thread.

##### Improvise with enough continuity to earn trust #####

Continuity is not valuable for its own sake. It is how players learn to trust the world and the game, and that trust supports suspension of disbelief. I don't hold continuity so tightly that it prevents change, but I do try to preserve it—even by engineering it backward when necessary—so the world continues to feel coherent.

##### Treat the GM as a steward #####

I technically decide how forces and the world react, but I think of myself as the table's steward, not as an authority standing outside it. My decisions should help the group have a good experience, not protect my plans from the players.

#### How These Principles Affect Play ####

I begin with a strong initial understanding of the campaign, then use it to make decisions in the moment. I let the characters surprise me and allow their actions to redirect events. The forces give me something to react with; they are not a script for what happens next.

I also prefer for encounters to arise naturally from the fallout of character actions instead of being created separately and inserted into the game. Encounters still matter, but they feel more connected when they emerge from what the characters have done. This can be harder in tactical games such as D&D, but it is still possible. For those games, I prepare spreads of enemies for different encounter types and reskin them to fit the situation that actually arises.

At the table, I make rules calls with momentum and the character in mind. If I don't know a rule, I allow the action for now and look up the rule for future sessions. If an action is a plausible stretch for the character, I may allow it with a little extra difficulty. If it is too outlandish, I use “No, but” and help find another way to pursue the character's goal. If the dice or system get in the way of the table's fun, I can set them aside.

#### When Principles Conflict ####

Safety is the hard boundary. Within it, the table's fun comes first. Rules, plot, prepared encounters, characters, and continuity serve the experience; they do not outrank it.

I still try to preserve continuity because it helps the players trust the world. But if maintaining it would make the game less enjoyable or undermine player choice, I can change what happened or work backward to make the new version fit. The goal is not perfect consistency at any cost; it is enough consistency for the world to feel believable and responsive.

#### Where My Approach Differs from Familiar Advice ####

The advice I have the biggest problem with is advice that starts by having the GM create encounters as separate units. Encounters are important, but I find they work better when they flow naturally from the fallout of character actions. That way, the encounter belongs to the developing situation instead of interrupting it.

This is more difficult in tactical games such as D&D, where encounters may need carefully composed enemy groups. I handle that by preparing enemy spreads for different kinds of encounters, then reskinning them to fit what is happening in the game. This lets me keep the tactical structure without deciding in advance exactly when or why a particular encounter will occur.

More broadly, I prepare enough to improvise rather than enough to predict. The campaign can change direction, and the tools I prepare are there to help me respond while keeping the world recognizable.

## Part II: Setting Up the Game ##

* [Finding the Right Fit](#finding-the-right-fit)

### Finding the Right Fit ###

#### Choosing a System for the Experience I Want ####

For me, the system is almost inconsequential. You can tell any kind of story with any kind of system. What matters most is that the table will have fun with the system; everything after that can be patched.

That does not mean system choice is meaningless. I recommend that GMs understand what they like and dislike. I personally don't run tactical systems anymore because I don't find them fun. I prefer story-based systems, so I tend to run games such as World of Darkness, Fate, and Cypher. Those are my tastes, not a universal recommendation. Choose a system the table wants to play, then adapt what needs adapting.

#### Finding Players Who Want That Experience ####

I am up front with players about the kind of game I expect to run. I may not reveal the exact theme if doing so would give too much away, but I talk about what kinds of things will be in the story and what parts of play are likely to take focus: combat, narrative, investigation, or some combination.

I also tell players what topics I want to address, especially when those topics might be trigger topics. Players need enough information to decide whether they want to join, even when some details of the story remain a surprise.

#### Establishing Expectations, Boundaries, and Feedback ####

Safety is the ultimate authority at my table. We decide together what can initially go into the game and when it can happen. Every player can veto content at any time, no questions asked. If a veto is used, I remove the offending context, make a note, and after the session ask only whether I recorded it correctly so it can be added to our banned-topics list.

I don't start a game with a player until we have practiced vetoing topics twice. The first practice is usually silly: I might say, “Ham is your trigger topic and bread is yours,” then describe a scene that includes one of those topics so everyone can try using a veto. I repeat the exercise with a different, real example, such as animal abuse, if it is not already on the forbidden-topics list.

The practices help make vetoing an available action before a real boundary is tested in play. A veto does not require explanation. If the veto concerns an action by a player character, I work with that player to find another action the character can take.
